Bob bought a house, but it needed some work. The previous owners had trouble paying their bills and lost the house to someone who fixed it up quickly and sold it for a higher price. When Bob moved in, he found that some of the repairs were just to make the house look better, not really fix it. For example, they put in new kitchen appliances but didn't upgrade the electrical system, which meant the power would go out every time Bob used his dishwasher and coffee machine at the same time. This cost Bob over $1,000 to fix.

The house flippers also covered up the old wooden floors with new carpet, which Bob didn't like so he ripped it out and had the floors refinished for another $3,000. The house was an old stucco house that got really hot in the summer and cold in the winter because of cheap windows. So Bob hired someone to install double pane storm windows and ceiling fans, which cost a few thousand more dollars.

To make the house more energy efficient, Bob leased solar panels for his roof. This saved him money on his electric bill and added value to the house. In two years, all the repairs and improvements he made to the house cost over $20,000. But during that same time, the value of his house went up by almost $100,000. Bob was happy because he knew when he sold the house, he would get more money than he paid for it.

Miami is renowned for its tropical climate, retiree community, and Cuban-American population, but not so much as an international art hub. However, the situation may change with billionaire real estate developer Jorge Pérez's plans to enhance downtown Miami's art scene.

Pérez, a passionate art lover and real estate tycoon, donated $40 million to the Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM), one of the few major institutions in the U.S. with a Hispanic name. This significant contribution will undoubtedly put Miami on the global art map.

Miami is undergoing a substantial transformation, particularly downtown, where David Beckham seeks to construct a stadium for his newly announced soccer team. Within the art world, Art Basel, an international art and fashion extravaganza that has taken place in Miami Beach for over a decade, is considered the country's leading art fair, attracting tens of thousands of visitors during its five-day event.

Pérez hopes his museum will elevate Miami to new heights in the art world. He believes cultural institutions have played a crucial role in the city's development, with PAMM as a prime example. Pérez started as an urban planner, focusing on affordable housing, before co-founding The Related Group of Florida and becoming known as the Condo King of South Florida. In 2005, TIME magazine recognized him as one of the top 25 most influential Hispanics in the United States.

Born in Argentina to Cuban parents, Pérez grew up in Colombia before moving to Miami as a teenager. His passion for Latin American art stems from his upbringing, and he began collecting works by notable artists such as Roberto Matta, Diego Rivera, Wifredo Lam, and Joaquin Torres-Garcia in his early twenties. Over 100 pieces from Pérez's personal collection are now on display inside the three-story, 200,000-square-foot museum designed by Pritzker Prize-winning Swiss architects Herzog & de Meuron.

The building boasts massive hurricane impact-resistant glass windows and over 70 self-watering hydroponic gardens designed by French landscape artist Patrick Blanc. The museum focuses on contemporary art from the 20th and 21st centuries, currently featuring Chinese artist-activist Ai Weiwei's According to What? collection.

PAMM is one of the main attractions in Museum Park, which will also house the Patricia and Phillip Frost Museum of Science set to open in 2015. The museum faced some controversy during its naming, with four board members resigning in protest over the decision to name it after Pérez instead of Miami Art Museum.

Despite the controversy, Pérez remains dedicated to the museum and is honored by the recognition. He sees his involvement as a way to contribute to causes he cares about and to be remembered for promoting them. PAMM has made significant progress in its $220 million capital campaign, reaching 90% of its goal.

People may have differing opinions on naming art museums after donors, but it seems that in Miami's case, the community values both art and science equally, as evidenced by the warm reception to the renaming of the Patricia and Phillip Frost Museum of Science after a generous donor.
